big_idea: We use rules + data to PREDICT future town outcomes.
learning_intention: We are learning to use a rule to predict a town outcome.
student_learning_goal: I can use a rule to predict a town outcome.
success_criteria: I can state a simple rule from data (e.g., 5 buses per day).
I can use the rule to predict a future outcome.
I can predict for different time spans (1 day, 5 days, 10 days).
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Mayor Mira and Town Tom — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 3 prediction tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Mayor Mira: 5 buses arrived each morning this week. Predict for 5 more days. Mira opens: 'PER day, PER week, PER MONTH — math grows with TIME!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Mayor Mira + Town Tom puppets. 'Friends — yesterday we collected DATA. Today we PREDICT what will happen NEXT.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write PREDICT on the chart. 'Predict means to say what we think will happen, using our DATA and a RULE.'

Demonstrate. 'Mayor Mira's data: 5 buses each morning Monday-Friday this week. The rule: 5 buses per day. Now predict for next week. Monday: 5. Tuesday: 5. Wednesday: 5. Thursday: 5. Friday: 5. Total: 25 buses next week.'

Write on the chart:
Rule: 5 buses per day.
Prediction: 25 buses for 5 days.

More examples:
Rule: 3 books per child per week. 24 children. Predict library books in 1 week → 72.
Rule: 15-minute recess. 4 recesses per week. Predict total recess time → 60 minutes.
Rule: 60 sandwiches sold per lunch. 5 lunches per week. Predict total → 300 sandwiches.

'Mayor Mira uses RULES from data to predict OUTCOMES. The bigger the time, the bigger the prediction.'

Now stretch. 'What if buses change? Sometimes 5, sometimes 6. Then our rule is APPROXIMATE. Predictions get more uncertain. We refine in Lesson 4.'

'Today we predict town outcomes for 1 day, 5 days, and 10 days.'
student_actions: Listen to Mayor Mira's prediction demo.

steps.instruction: Whole group: predict outcomes for 4 rules. (a) 5 buses per day → 5, 25, 50. (b) 3 books per child → 72 weekly for 24 kids. (c) 15-min recess x 4 → 60 min weekly. (d) 60 sandwiches per lunch x 5 → 300 weekly.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Use the rule. Predict for 1, 5, 10 days.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: One Rule, Many Times — pair takes 1 rule (5 buses/day) and predicts for 1, 3, 5, 10 days. Station B: One Day, Many Rules — pair takes 1 day and predicts for 4 different town situations. Station C: My Town Rule — pair invents a rule from their town (e.g., 2 swings at the park) and predicts for a week.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: invent a 2-rule prediction (e.g., 5 buses morning + 5 buses afternoon = 10 buses per day).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to extending pairs: 'Stretch: 2-rule prediction. Show your work.'

steps.instruction: Discuss prediction logic. 'Predictions multiply rules by time. Rule x time = prediction. The rule doesn't change; the time spans do.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show the modelling chart. 'Step 3 of modelling: PREDICT. Use data + rule to predict outcomes.'

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the prediction tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'What's your rule? What's your prediction?' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only single-day predictions.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a structured frame: 'My rule: ___. For ___ days, my prediction is ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Use the number line as a floor mat. Walk forward 5 steps for each day.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: states a rule; predicts for a given time span; predicts for multiple time spans.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the prediction tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: How do we use a rule to predict?
Can predictions ever be wrong? When?
What's a prediction you'd make about your town?
consolidation.exit_routine: Mayor Mira's prediction refrain — class chants: 'PER day, PER week, PER MONTH — math grows with TIME!' Each child writes ONE prediction with the rate citation.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 3 captures C4 step 3 (predict). Children at L4 apply rules across multiple time spans accurately.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child predicts the same number for any time span — repairing the time-doesn't-multiply trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
When children predict from town data (Day 3 task: 5 buses today, how many tomorrow?), a real Grade-2 trap is the rate-as-state confusion (Thompson & Saldanha 2003, 'Fractions and Multiplicative Reasoning'): child treats '5 buses/day' as a static fact rather than a rate that scales over multiple days. Carpenter & Moser CGI 'measurement-rate' problem types name this directly.

Yesterday's tally (Lesson 2) is the data backbone. Today we stretch it forward: same rate, more days. Tomorrow (Lesson 4) we reflect and refine; Day 5 capstones the full cycle.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Rule: 5 buses per day. Child predicts 5 buses for 5 days.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'You said 5 buses for 5 days. But that's only 1 day's worth! For 5 days, we need 5 buses x 5 days.'

The child looks confused. 'Each day = 5 buses. Day 1: 5. Day 2: 5. Day 3: 5. Day 4: 5. Day 5: 5. Add them up.' Walk through. 5+5+5+5+5 = 25. 'So for 5 days, the prediction is 25 buses.'

Generalise. 'Mayor Mira's formula: RULE per day x NUMBER of days = PREDICTION. Multiply, don't keep the same.'

Now another. '3 books per child per week, 24 children, 1 week → 3 x 24 = 72 books.' Practice the multiplication.

If the child STILL doesn't multiply: provide a chart with explicit slots. 'Day 1: ___. Day 2: ___. Total: ___.' Add column by column.

Long-term recovery: every prediction task uses 'rule x time'. Build the multiplication-with-time reflex.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Predicts the same for any time span.
(Mid) Multiplies with prompts; uses repeated addition.
(Strong) Multiplies independently; predicts for multiple spans.
common_misconceptions: Time doesn't matter. (Repair: prediction multiplies rule by time.)
Repeated addition is wrong. (Repair: repeated addition is one path to multiplication.)
I just say the rule. (Repair: prediction is rule x time, not just the rule.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child treats rate as static (5 buses/day → 5 buses across all days): point at the per-day tally; ask 'how many ALTOGETHER over 3 days?' Child re-counts.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child can multiply but not articulate the rate: drill 'PER day' language explicitly — '5 buses PER day for 3 days = 15.'
DIAGNOSTIC C — child predicts but won't justify with data: force the data citation — 'Show me the row in the tally that supports your prediction.'

parts_outline.task: Use the rule '5 buses per day'. Predict for 1, 3, 5, 10 days.
Use 4 different town rules. Predict outcomes for 1 week.
Pick your own town rule. Predict for 5 days.
